messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Redirection: I think of something else, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ana Gómez had always taken pride in her work as a detective. For over two decades, she had been driven by a strong sense of justice and a determination to protect others. But all that changed on the day she was exposed to toxic chemicals while investigating a warehouse fire. The memories of that event still felt like they were happening right now - not just fragments, but the sensations, too: the feeling of her airway constricting as she struggled to breathe, the smell of sweat and antiseptic that clung to her skin. In the months following the incident, Ana began to notice subtle changes in herself. She was more jumpy than usual, always on edge when unexpected sounds caught her off guard - a car backfiring, a door slamming shut. Her colleagues started to comment on how tense she seemed all the time, like her body was coiled and ready to spring into action at any moment. Ana couldn't shake the feeling that danger lurked around every corner, waiting to pounce. As a detective, Ana had always relied on her sharp instincts to scan for potential threats. But now, this hyper-vigilance seemed more like a curse than a blessing. She found herself constantly scanning her surroundings, even when she was off-duty - in the grocery store, at home with her family. Her ex-husband had complained about it during their divorce proceedings, saying that Ana's constant "on-edge" behavior had made him feel like he was walking on eggshells around her. Ana tried to push these feelings away by redirecting her thoughts whenever they arose. She'd focus on something else - a case she was working on, a TV show she liked - but the tension remained, simmering just below the surface. And then there were the triggers: certain smells could send her spiraling back into that warehouse, gasping for air. Sweat or body odor would transport her to the hospital where she'd spent weeks recovering from her exposure, feeling helpless and scared. The worst part was when Ana caught sight of authority figures - police officers, firefighters, even medical personnel in their crisp uniforms. She knew it didn't make sense; these were people who were supposed to help others, just like she did. But something about their confidence and composure triggered a deep-seated anxiety within her. It made her feel lost, like she was floating outside of herself, unable to reconnect with the world around her. Ana had always prided herself on being stoic, unflappable in the face of danger. But now, even small setbacks sent her reeling. She felt like a part of her had been irreparably damaged during that warehouse fire - not just her lungs, but something deeper and more fundamental to who she was as a person. One day, while investigating a routine case, Ana found herself standing outside the hospital where she'd spent so many weeks recovering from her exposure. Something about the sight and smell of it sent her tumbling backward in time, her memories colliding with each other like jagged pieces of glass. She stumbled away from the scene, feeling raw and exposed. For a while after that incident, Ana tried to hide behind her mask of professionalism, but the truth was starting to seep out: she couldn't do this anymore. The constant hypervigilance, the triggers that sent her careening back into the past - it was all taking its toll on her relationships and her work. That's when Ana finally realized she needed help. She scheduled an appointment with a therapist, terrified of facing what lay ahead but knowing she couldn't keep running from herself forever. What frightened Ana most was that she'd lost touch with her emotions, like they were locked away behind some impenetrable wall. She longed to feel whole again - not just as a detective, but as a person.
